answer.mechanism_primary: PRMT7 restrains NF-kB non-catalytically: the PRMT7 protein itself binds p65/RelA and holds it in the cytoplasm, so the restraint is set by how much PRMT7 protein is present and is relieved only when the protein is removed (gene deletion or PROTAC degradation), not when its methyltransferase activity is blocked.
key_entities: protein removal (deletion, PROTAC) versus catalytic-site occupancy

rationale: Three manipulations of one protein split two to one, and the split is informative because the two that work remove PRMT7 protein while the one that does not leaves the protein in place. The deletion removes it genetically; the PROTAC removes it post-translationally, recruiting VHL so the proteasome destroys it, with Prmt7 mRNA untouched and the effect blocked by MG132 and MLN4924. Both raise nuclear p65 and expand the CD8+ compartment. The catalytic inhibitor occupies the active site and leaves PRMT7 standing, and it does not expand CD8+ cells. The first thing to rule out is a technical failure of that arm: it is not one, because pre-dosing cells with the inhibitor stops the degrader from destroying PRMT7, which can only happen if the inhibitor is sitting on PRMT7 inside the cell. So the inhibitor arm is a real test of catalysis, and catalysis is not what the other two arms take away. What they take away is the protein itself. That fits what PRMT7 does to p65 here: it is a cytoplasmic protein, it is found in p65 immunoprecipitates from T cells, and raising it increases cytoplasmic p65. Read together, these say the restraint is a binding function - PRMT7 holds p65 in the cytoplasm - and binding is a property of the protein, available whether or not the enzyme is turning over. The brake is therefore stoichiometric: it scales with how much PRMT7 protein is present, which is why degrading or deleting it releases p65 while blocking its catalytic site does not. Release then favours CD8+ cells rather than killing them, because in PRMT7-deficient CD8+ T cells the NF-kB targets that rise include the survival genes Bcl-2 and Bcl-xL and CD25, apoptosis programmes fall, and the CD8+ difference disappears when NF-kB is inhibited with BAY 11-7082. The prediction follows: anything that lowers PRMT7 protein de-represses NF-kB and expands CD8+ cells, and anything that only blocks its methyltransferase activity does not. Why blocking catalysis actively reduced the CD8+ fraction is a separate question these results do not settle.
